claim: Robust chromosome biorientation requires progressive restriction of attachment geometry.
source: Robust chromosome biorientation requires progressive restriction of attachment geometry, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and attachment force dependence.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that progressive restriction is essential for biorientation in the model.

claim: Robust chromosome biorientation requires destabilization of misaligned attachments.
source: Robust chromosome biorientation requires progressive restriction of attachment geometry, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and attachment force dependence.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that error correction through destabilization is essential for biorientation.

claim: Robust chromosome biorientation requires attachment force dependence.
source: Robust chromosome biorientation requires progressive restriction of attachment geometry, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and attachment force dependence.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that force-dependent attachment kinetics are essential for maintaining biorientation.

claim: Large spindle length fluctuations can occur when the kinetochore-microtubule attachment lifetime is long.
source: Large spindle length fluctuations can occur when the kinetochore-microtubule attachment lifetime is long.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing correlation between attachment lifetime and spindle length fluctuations.

claim: The primary spindle force generators are kinesin-5 motors and crosslinkers in early mitosis.
source: The primary spindle force generators are kinesin-5 motors and crosslinkers in early mitosis, while interkinetochore stretch becomes important after biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model showing that motors and crosslinkers dominate force generation early in spindle assembly.

claim: Interkinetochore stretch becomes important after biorientation.
source: The primary spindle force generators are kinesin-5 motors and crosslinkers in early mitosis, while interkinetochore stretch becomes important after biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model showing that chromosome force becomes significant after biorientation.

claim: The same mechanisms that contribute to persistent biorientation lead to segregation of chromosomes to the poles after anaphase onset.
source: The same mechanisms that contribute to persistent biorientation lead to segregation of chromosomes to the poles after anaphase onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing that few additional mechanisms are required for chromosome segregation beyond those used for biorientation.

claim: Dynamic spindle MTs are typically organized with their plus-ends toward the center of the spindle, forming a bipolar array as the spindle poles move apart.
source: Dynamic spindle MTs are typically organized with their plus-ends toward the center of the spindle, forming a bipolar array as the spindle poles move apart (Figure 1; Taylor, 1959; McIntosh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle structure.

claim: Motor proteins and crosslinkers that bundle and slide MTs create, extend, and stabilize MT bundles.
source: Motor proteins and crosslinkers that bundle and slide MTs create, extend, and stabilize MT bundles (Figure 1A,B; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Pidoux et al., 1996; Chen et al., 2012; Hepperla et al., 2014; Hueschen et al., 2019; Yamashita et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007; Braun et al., 2011; Lansky et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on motor protein and crosslinker function.

claim: Biorientation occurs when sister kinetochores are attached to sister poles, but is often preceded by erroneous attachment.
source: Biorientation occurs when sister kinetochores are attached to sister poles, but is often preceded by erroneous attachment (Figure 1D; Cimini et al., 2001; Salmon et al., 2005; Rumpf et al., 2010; Gregan et al., 2011; Lampson and Grishchuk, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on chromosome biorientation and attachment errors.

claim: Kinetochores link chromosomes to MTs.
source: Kinetochores therefore perform multiple functions: they link chromosomes to MTs, maintain attachment to MT ends under force and as MTs grow and shrink, sense MT attachment and tension between sisters, and regulate correction of attachment errors and the spindle-assembly checkpoint (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore function.

claim: Kinetochores maintain attachment to MT ends under force and as MTs grow and shrink.
source: Kinetochores therefore perform multiple functions: they link chromosomes to MTs, maintain attachment to MT ends under force and as MTs grow and shrink, sense MT attachment and tension between sisters, and regulate correction of attachment errors and the spindle-assembly checkpoint (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore function.

claim: Kinetochores sense MT attachment and tension between sisters.
source: Kinetochores therefore perform multiple functions: they link chromosomes to MTs, maintain attachment to MT ends under force and as MTs grow and shrink, sense MT attachment and tension between sisters, and regulate correction of attachment errors and the spindle-assembly checkpoint (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore function.

claim: Kinetochores regulate correction of attachment errors and the spindle-assembly checkpoint.
source: Kinetochores therefore perform multiple functions: they link chromosomes to MTs, maintain attachment to MT ends under force and as MTs grow and shrink, sense MT attachment and tension between sisters, and regulate correction of attachment errors and the spindle-assembly checkpoint (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore function.

claim: Error correction is affected by kinetochore geometry.
source: Error correction is affected by kinetochore geometry (Gregan et al., 2007; Paul et al., 2009; Rumpf et al., 2010; Magidson et al., 2015; Zaytsev and Grishchuk, 2015) and attachment/tension sensing (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Salmon and Bloom, 2017), although the relative contribution of different effects is not established (Nannas and Murray, 2014; Tauchman et al., 2015; Kuhn and Dumont, 2017; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on error correction mechanisms.

claim: Error correction is affected by attachment/tension sensing.
source: Error correction is affected by kinetochore geometry (Gregan et al., 2007; Paul et al., 2009; Rumpf et al., 2010; Magidson et al., 2015; Zaytsev and Grishchuk, 2015) and attachment/tension sensing (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Salmon and Bloom, 2017), although the relative contribution of different effects is not established (Nannas and Murray, 2014; Tauchman et al., 2015; Kuhn and Dumont, 2017; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on error correction mechanisms.

claim: The relative contribution of different effects to error correction is not established.
source: Error correction is affected by kinetochore geometry (Gregan et al., 2007; Paul et al., 2009; Rumpf et al., 2010; Magidson et al., 2015; Zaytsev and Grishchuk, 2015) and attachment/tension sensing (Sacristan and Kops, 2015; Musacchio, 2015; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Salmon and Bloom, 2017), although the relative contribution of different effects is not established (Nannas and Murray, 2014; Tauchman et al., 2015; Kuhn and Dumont, 2017; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature indicating uncertainty about relative contributions.

claim: Destabilization of incorrect attachments by Aurora B kinase appears to be particularly important for high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
source: Destabilization of incorrect attachments by Aurora B kinase appears to be particularly important for high-fidelity chromosome segregation (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Cimini et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Aurora B kinase function.

claim: The spindle achieves a consistent length once it assembles and attaches to chromosomes.
source: Once the spindle assembles and attaches to chromosomes, it achieves a consistent length (Dumont and Mitchison, 2009; Goshima and Scholey, 2010; Nannas et al., 2014; Rizk et al., 2014; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length regulation.

claim: The force-balance model proposes that outward-directed forces from plus-end directed sliding motors separate spindle poles, while inward-directed forces from minus-end directed sliding motors and chromosomes pull the poles together.
source: The force-balance model proposes that outward-directed forces from plus-end directed sliding motors separate spindle poles, while inward-directed forces from minus-end directed sliding motors and chromosomes pull the poles together (Saunders and Hoyt, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original force-balance model.

claim: The force-balance model helps explain perturbations that alter spindle length.
source: This model helps explain perturbations that alter spindle length (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Hepperla et al., 2014; Chacón et al., 2014; Nannas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length perturbations.

claim: A change in spindle length may occur from a direct change in force production or from indirect effects such as alteration in MT dynamics or alignment.
source: However, a change in spindle length may occur from a direct change in force production or from indirect effects such as alteration in MT dynamics or alignment (Hepperla et al., 2014; Gergely et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length changes.

claim: Fission-yeast double mutants can have wild-type average metaphase spindle length, but much larger fluctuations than wild-type.
source: Remarkably, fission-yeast double mutants can have wild-type average metaphase spindle length, but much larger fluctuations than wild-type (Syrovatkina et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on fission-yeast mutants.

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe cells are amenable to genetic manipulation and quantitative experiments.
source: Schizosaccharomyces pombe cells are amenable to genetic manipulation and quantitative experiments (Ward et al., 2015; Mary et al., 2015; Klemm et al., 2018; Blackwell et al., 2017b; Blackwell et al., 2017a) and the spindles are small enough that full 3D simulations are computationally tractable (Glunčić et al., 2015; Ward et al., 2015; Blackwell et al., 2017a; Lamson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on S. pombe experimental methods.

claim: S. pombe spindles are small enough that full 3D simulations are computationally tractable.
source: Schizosaccharomyces pombe cells are amenable to genetic manipulation and quantitative experiments (Ward et al., 2015; Mary et al., 2015; Klemm et al., 2018; Blackwell et al., 2017b; Blackwell et al., 2017a) and the spindles are small enough that full 3D simulations are computationally tractable (Glunčić et al., 2015; Ward et al., 2015; Blackwell et al., 2017a; Lamson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on computational modeling of S. pombe spindles.

claim: The model successfully accomplishes spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation.
source: Our model successfully accomplishes spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model emphasizes the importance of progressive restriction of attachment for error correction and long-lived biorientation.
source: The results give insight into key requirements for error correction and long-lived biorientation, emphasizing the importance of progressive restriction of attachment, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and force-dependent attachment lifetime.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the necessity of progressive restriction.

claim: The model emphasizes the importance of destabilization of misaligned attachments for error correction and long-lived biorientation.
source: The results give insight into key requirements for error correction and long-lived biorientation, emphasizing the importance of progressive restriction of attachment, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and force-dependent attachment lifetime.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the necessity of misaligned destabilization.

claim: The model emphasizes the importance of force-dependent attachment lifetime for error correction and long-lived biorientation.
source: The results give insight into key requirements for error correction and long-lived biorientation, emphasizing the importance of progressive restriction of attachment, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and force-dependent attachment lifetime.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the necessity of force-dependent attachment kinetics.

claim: The turnover of kinetochore-MT attachments affects spindle mechanics.
source: The turnover of kinetochore-MT attachments affects spindle mechanics, because models with larger attachment lifetime exhibit larger fluctuations in spindle length.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing correlation between attachment lifetime and spindle length fluctuations.

claim: Models with larger attachment lifetime exhibit larger fluctuations in spindle length.
source: The turnover of kinetochore-MT attachments affects spindle mechanics, because models with larger attachment lifetime exhibit larger fluctuations in spindle length.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing correlation between attachment lifetime and spindle length fluctuations.

claim: Properly constructed metaphase spindles are able to robustly segregate chromosomes in the model.
source: Finally, properly constructed metaphase spindles are able to robustly segregate chromosomes in the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing chromosome segregation.

claim: The model uses three-dimensional geometry and an initial condition with side-by-side centrosomes that mimics the biological configuration at the onset of mitosis.
source: In developing the model, we used three-dimensional geometry and an initial condition with side-by-side centrosomes (spindle-pole bodies, or SPBs) that mimics the biological configuration at the onset of mitosis.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Stochastic binding kinetics and turnover of motor proteins, crosslinkers, and kinetochore-MT attachments are important in spindle assembly and chromosome alignment.
source: Because stochastic binding kinetics and turnover of motor proteins, crosslinkers, and kinetochore-MT attachments are important in spindle assembly and chromosome alignment, we developed methods to rapidly compute the statistical mechanics of protein binding and unbinding (Gao et al., 2015b; Gao et al., 2015a; Blackwell et al., 2016; Blackwell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is a rationale for the modeling approach.

claim: The binding and unbinding of motors, crosslinkers, and kinetochore-MT attachments is microscopically reversible and force-dependent.
source: The binding and unbinding of motors, crosslinkers, and kinetochore-MT attachments is microscopically reversible and force-dependent.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Motor proteins move with force-dependent velocity, which can be important for force generation by crosslinking motors.
source: Motor proteins move with force-dependent velocity, which can be important for force generation by crosslinking motors (Blackwell et al., 2016; Blackwell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is a description of the model.

claim: The simulation takes place within a sphere that represents the fission-yeast nucleus.
source: The simulation takes place within a sphere that represents the fission-yeast nucleus.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Two SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope but free to move on the surface of the sphere.
source: Two SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope but free to move on the surface of the sphere (although we also consider effects of allowing SPBs to move radially due to a soft nuclear envelope in one variant of the model, as discussed below).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Each SPB nucleates 14 MTs, with their minus-ends tethered to the SPBs by a spring and which undergo dynamic instability at their plus-ends.
source: Each SPB nucleates 14 MTs, with their minus-ends tethered to the SPBs by a spring and which undergo dynamic instability at their plus-ends.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Kinesin-5 motors move bidirectionally on MTs.
source: Kinesin-5 motors (representing Cut7) move bidirectionally on MTs (Edamatsu, 2014; Edamatsu, 2016; Britto et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018), with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs exerting force to slide apart the SPBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 motor behavior.

claim: Kinesin-5 motors exert force to slide apart the SPBs with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs.
source: Kinesin-5 motors (representing Cut7) move bidirectionally on MTs (Edamatsu, 2014; Edamatsu, 2016; Britto et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018), with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs exerting force to slide apart the SPBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claim: Kinesin-14 motors crosslink MTs and one head walks toward the MT minus-ends, aligning MTs and exerting force that shortens the spindle.
source: Kinesin-14 motors (representing Pkl1 and Klp2) crosslink MTs and one head walks toward the MT minus-ends, aligning MTs and exerting force that shortens the spindle (Pidoux et al., 1996; Troxell et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2012; Olmsted et al., 2014; Hepperla et al., 2014; Yukawa et al., 2015; Yukawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-14 motor behavior.

claim: Crosslinkers preferentially bind antiparallel MTs.
source: Crosslinkers (representing Ase1) preferentially bind antiparallel MTs (Yamashita et al., 2005; Loïodice et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007; Kapitein et al., 2008; Courtheoux et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2009) and stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP (Bratman and Chang, 2007) to MT ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on crosslinker behavior.

claim: Crosslinkers stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP to MT ends.
source: Crosslinkers (representing Ase1) preferentially bind antiparallel MTs (Yamashita et al., 2005; Loïodice et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007; Kapitein et al., 2008; Courtheoux et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2009) and stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP (Bratman and Chang, 2007) to MT ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claim: Fission-yeast kinetochores can bind up to 3 MTs.
source: Because fission-yeast kinetochores can bind up to 3 MTs (Ding et al., 1993), each kinetochore has three attachment factors in the model separated by 40 nm along the kinetochore plate (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinetochore structure.

claim: Attachment factors can make both lateral and end-on attachments to MTs, with different binding kinetics that favor end-on attachment.
source: Attachment factors can make both lateral and end-on attachments to MTs, with different binding kinetics that favor end-on attachment.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: The model includes tip tracking: a tip-bound attachment factor tracks MT ends by maintaining end-on attachment during MT growth and shrinking.
source: Importantly, the model includes tip tracking: a tip-bound attachment factor tracks MT ends by maintaining end-on attachment during MT growth and shrinking.
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: End-on attachment alters MT dynamic instability and is force-dependent, as measured previously.
source: End-on attachment alters MT dynamic instability and is force-dependent, as measured previously (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore-MT attachment.

claim: Sister kinetochores are linked via springs that resist stretching and rotation, to maintain the distance and alignment of the kinetochores.
source: Sister kinetochores are linked via springs that resist stretching and rotation, to maintain the distance and alignment of the kinetochores (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 1; Mary et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claim: The pericentric DNA is modeled as a spherocylinder of length 200 nm and diameter 75 nm, which has a soft repulsion with MTs that allows MT-chromatin overlap with an energy penalty.
source: The pericentric DNA is modeled as a spherocylinder of length 200 nm and diameter 75 nm, which has a soft repulsion with MTs that allows MT-chromatin overlap with an energy penalty (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: The model can achieve both correct and erroneous kinetochore-MT attachment states.
source: With these ingredients, the model can achieve both correct and erroneous kinetochore-MT attachment states (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three key model ingredients were required to achieve error correction and persistent biorientation: progressive restriction of attachment, destabilization of misaligned attachment, and stabilization of attachment by force.
source: To achieve error correction and persistent biorientation, we found three key model ingredients were required: progressive restriction of attachment (Figure 1E), destabilization of misaligned attachment (Figure 1F), and stabilization of attachment by force (Figure 1G, Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the necessity of these three mechanisms.

claim: The model exhibits both spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation.
source: With these mechanisms, the model exhibits both spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation (Figure 1H, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1H and Video 1.

claim: Simulations of the reference model showed dynamics of SPB separation, kinetochore movement along the spindle, and interkinetochore stretch similar to the experimental data.
source: After refinement, simulations of the reference model showed dynamics of SPB separation, kinetochore movement along the spindle, and interkinetochore stretch similar to the experimental data (Figure 2E–H, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe.
source: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe, and temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies (Hagan and Yanagida, 1990; Hagan and Yanagida, 1992; Yukawa et al., 2018; Toda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 function.

claim: Temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies.
source: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe, and temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies (Hagan and Yanagida, 1990; Hagan and Yanagida, 1992; Yukawa et al., 2018; Toda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 mutants.

claim: When kinesin-5 is removed from the model, SPBs do not separate.
source: Consistent with this, when we remove kinesin-5 from the model, SPBs do not separate (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The microtubule-associated protein CLASP is essential for spindle assembly in fission yeast, where it is recruited to MT antiparallel overlaps by Ase1 and stabilizes MT dynamics.
source: Similarly, the microtubule-associated protein CLASP is essential for spindle assembly in fission yeast, where it is recruited to MT antiparallel overlaps by Ase1 and stabilizes MT dynamics (Bratman and Chang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on CLASP function.

claim: When the stabilization of dynamics of crosslinked MTs is turned off in the model, SPBs do not separate.
source: When the stabilization of dynamics of crosslinked MTs is turned off in the model, SPBs do not separate (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Chromosome biorientation is abolished in models where the SPBs do not separate.
source: Chromosome biorientation is abolished in models where the SPBs do not separate (Figure 2L, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2L and Video 2.

claim: Cells lacking Klp2 or both Pkl1 and Klp2 do not show altered average spindle length.
source: Experimentally, cells lacking Klp2 or both Pkl1 and Klp2 do not show altered average spindle length (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Troxell et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-14 mutants.

claim: Model spindles formed and bioriented chromosomes in the absence of kinesin-14, and spindle length depended on the ratio of kinesin-5 to crosslinkers.
source: Consistent with this, model spindles formed and bioriented chromosomes in the absence of kinesin-14, and spindle length depended on the ratio of kinesin-5 to crosslinkers.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Ase1 deletion cells assemble spindles in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast, Ase1 deletion cells assemble spindles (Yamashita et al., 2005; Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Yukawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Ase1 deletion.

claim: Removing crosslinkers in the reference model abolished spindle assembly because spindles cannot maintain robust antiparallel MT overlaps.
source: Removing crosslinkers in the reference model abolished spindle assembly because spindles cannot maintain robust antiparallel MT overlaps.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: In the reference model the kinesin-14 motors are highly sensitive to force-dependent unbinding: the characteristic distance that quantifies this is 3.2 times larger for kinesin-14 motors than kinesin-5 motors.
source: However, in the reference model the kinesin-14 motors are highly sensitive to force-dependent unbinding: the characteristic distance that quantifies this is 3.2 times larger for kinesin-14 motors than kinesin-5 motors.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: When kinesin-14 motors are modeled with the same force sensitivity to unbinding as for the kinesin-5 motors, spindle formation and chromosome biorientation are rescued.
source: When we model the kinesin-14 motors with the same force sensitivity to unbinding as for the kinesin-5 motors, spindle formation and chromosome biorientation are rescued (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles.
source: The results show that a soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3), but for a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 3.

claim: For a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
source: The results show that a soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3), but for a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental measurements.

claim: Biorientation requires the model to correct attachment errors and maintain correct attachments.
source: Biorientation requires the model to correct attachment errors and maintain correct attachments.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Biorientation occurs in the simulations primarily through progressive restriction of attachment angle, misaligned destabilization, and force-dependent kinetochore-MT attachment.
source: This occurs in the simulations primarily through progressive restriction of attachment angle, misaligned destabilization, and force-dependent kinetochore-MT attachment.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the importance of these three mechanisms.

claim: The model progressively restricts the angle at which binding can occur as more MTs bind to facilitate correct initial attachment of MTs to kinetochores.
source: To facilitate correct initial attachment of MTs to kinetochores, the model progressively restricts the angle at which binding can occur as more MTs bind (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Progressive restriction is motivated by previous work demonstrating that kinetochore geometry and chromosome rotation play an important role in promoting correct kinetochore-MT attachment and correcting errors.
source: This is motivated by previous work demonstrating that kinetochore geometry and chromosome rotation play an important role in promoting correct kinetochore-MT attachment and correcting errors (Gregan et al., 2007; Rumpf et al., 2010; Paul et al., 2009; Magidson et al., 2015; Zaytsev and Grishchuk, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore geometry and error correction.

claim: Unattached kinetochores have a wide angular range over which attachments can form.
source: In our model, unattached kinetochores have a wide angular range over which attachments can form (modeled as an angular spring constant for binding, represented by the three wide cones in Figure 1E left).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: Each attachment formed narrows the angle allowed for the subsequent attachment, favoring attachment to MTs that are more perpendicular to the kinetochore plate.
source: Each attachment formed narrows the angle allowed for the subsequent attachment, favoring attachment to MTs that are more perpendicular to the kinetochore plate (represented by the narrower cones in Figure 1E right).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claim: When attachment angle is most permissive, merotelic attachments form and are not corrected sufficiently rapidly to biorient the chromosomes.
source: These failures occur for different reasons as the angular spring constant varies. When attachment angle is most permissive, merotelic attachments form and are not corrected sufficiently rapidly to biorient the chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: When the attachment angle is highly restricted, attachments are unlikely to form at all.
source: When the attachment angle is highly restricted, attachments are unlikely to form at all.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Progressive restriction of attachment is essential for biorientation in the model.
source: Overall, this result shows that in our model progressive restriction of attachment is essential for biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing that removing progressive restriction abolishes biorientation.

claim: For the first attachment, promoting kinetochore binding to any MT is important: initial attachments should be established easily, even if erroneous.
source: This means that for the first attachment, promoting kinetochore binding to any MT is important: initial attachments should be established easily, even if erroneous.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Biorientation is increased when the third (final) binding event is highly restricted.
source: By contrast, biorientation is increased when the third (final) binding event is highly restricted (Figure 3C): chromosomes are bioriented in the model <10% of the time when the third attachment is most permissive, but the fraction of simultaneous biorientation increases with the angular stiffness of the third binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The second value of the angular potential for progressive restriction was less important.
source: The second value of the angular potential for progressive restriction was less important (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A): varying it did not significantly change the fraction of simultaneous biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Varying the number of allowed kinetochore-MT attachments does not significantly affect how easily biorientation is achieved.
source: Because of the importance of progressive restriction in our model, we additionally examined whether varying the number of allowed kinetochore-MT attachments might affect how easily biorientation is achieved, but found no significant effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time.
source: Previous experimental work has shown that merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time (Cimini et al., 2003) due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase (DeLuca et al., 2006; Cimini et al., 2006; Gay et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on merotelic attachments and error correction.

claim: Merotelic attachments are corrected over time due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase.
source: Previous experimental work has shown that merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time (Cimini et al., 2003) due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase (DeLuca et al., 2006; Cimini et al., 2006; Gay et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Aurora B kinase function.

claim: Experimental work has demonstrated a decrease in kinetochore MT turnover by up to a factor of 65 in the presence of Aurora B inhibitors.
source: Because experimental work has demonstrated a decrease in kinetochore MT turnover by up to a factor of 65 in the presence of Aurora B inhibitors (Cimini et al., 2006), we varied the misaligned destabilization factor in the model, which quantifies the increased turnover of incorrect attachments, over a similar range from 1 to 100 (Figure 3D, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Aurora B inhibitors.

claim: Biorientation is nearly eliminated in the absence of misaligned destabilization.
source: Consistent with experimental results, biorientation is nearly eliminated in the absence of misaligned destabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Biorientation time in the model is maximum when the misaligned destabilization factor is 70, comparable to the experimental value.
source: Biorientation time in the model is maximum when the misaligned destabilization factor is 70, comparable to the experimental value.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and comparison to experimental values.

claim: Misaligned destabilization demonstrates the importance of error correction in the model.
source: This demonstrates the importance of error correction in the model.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Kinetochore-MT attachments are stabilized by force.
source: We therefore additionally tested a force-dependent error correction model, based on previous results that kinetochore-MT attachments are stabilized by force (Nicklas and Koch, 1969; Cane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claim: The force-stabilization model of error correction experiences the initial problem of biorientation (IPBO): a bioriented attachment that has just formed is not under tension, and therefore is not stable.
source: The force-stabilization model of error correction that we implemented experiences the initial problem of biorientation (IPBO): a bioriented attachment that has just formed is not under tension, and therefore is not stable (Zhang et al., 2013; Kalantzaki et al., 2015; Tubman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on the IPBO and is an inference from the model construction.

claim: Implementing force-dependent stabilization alone did not lead to biorientation.
source: Consistent with this, we found implementing force-dependent stabilization alone did not lead to biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The IPBO may be solved by initial syntelic-like attachments that are end-on between the kinetochore face near a pole, and lateral to the kinetochore farther from that same pole.
source: Recent work has suggested that the IPBO may be solved by initial syntelic-like attachments that are end-on between the kinetochore face near a pole, and lateral to the kinetochore farther from that same pole (Kuhn and Dumont, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on solving the IPBO.

claim: Long-lived biorientation was achieved in the force-dependent error correction model with model parameters that favored end-on over lateral attachments, inhibited attachments at high angle, and allowed sister kinetochores to more easily reorient.
source: We were able to achieve long-lived biorientation in the force-dependent error correction model with model parameters that favored end-on over lateral attachments, inhibited attachments at high angle, and allowed sister kinetochores to more easily reorient (Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The model is sensitive to the value of the characteristic force that controls how much attachments are stabilized by force, with best performance of the model at a characteristic force of 1.67 pN.
source: We found that the model is sensitive to the value of this characteristic force, with best performance of the model at a characteristic force of 1.67 pN.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Higher or lower values of the characteristic force decrease cumulative biorientation by up to a factor of two.
source: Higher or lower values decrease cumulative biorientation by up to a factor of two.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Attachments between single MTs and purified budding-yeast kinetochores were altered by force applied to the kinetochore, even in the absence of Aurora kinase.
source: Attachments between single MTs and purified budding-yeast kinetochores were altered by force applied to the kinetochore, even in the absence of Aurora kinase (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claim: The kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime increased with tension when kinetochores were attached to depolymerizing MTs, an effect dependent on a TOG protein.
source: In particular, the kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime increased with tension when kinetochores were attached to depolymerizing MTs, an effect dependent on a TOG protein (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claim: Force dependence of attachments is required to maintain biorientation in the model.
source: Consistent with this, we implemented force dependence of attachments in the model (Figure 1G). This effect is required to maintain biorientation: if we eliminate the force dependence of attachment kinetics, biorientation is nearly abolished in the model (Figure 3F, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3F and Video 4.

claim: The increase in attachment lifetime of a kinetochore bound to a shrinking MT is the key force-dependent rate for maintaining biorientation.
source: To understand which force-dependent rate is most important for this effect, we added them back to the model one at a time. The increase in attachment lifetime of a kinetochore bound to a shrinking MT is the key force-dependent rate, because making this the only force-dependent lifetime in the model restores nearly all biorientation compared to the model with all rates force-dependent (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Maintenance of biorientation requires kinetochore-MT attachments to persist during MT depolymerization.
source: This demonstrates that maintenance of biorientation requires kinetochore-MT attachments to persist during MT depolymerization.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: One key determinant of the magnitude of spindle length fluctuations is the lifetime of kinetochore-MT attachments.
source: One key determinant of the magnitude of spindle length fluctuations is the lifetime of kinetochore-MT attachments (Figure 4, Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4 and Video 6.

claim: The magnitude of length fluctuations increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime: the longer the lifetime, the larger the fluctuations.
source: This measure of length fluctuations increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime: the longer the lifetime, the larger the fluctuations (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: For long-lived attachment, the force exerted by a stretched kinetochore can grow over time to a larger value: long-lived attachment allows multiple MTs to bind per kinetochore, exert greater force, and stretch apart the sisters.
source: To understand this result, note that for long-lived attachment, the force exerted by a stretched kinetochore can grow over time to a larger value: long-lived attachment allows multiple MTs to bind per kinetochore, exert greater force, and stretch apart the sisters.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The average interkinetochore distance increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime.
source: Indeed, the average interkinetochore distance increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Slow cycles of attachment and detachment lead to slowly varying force on the spindle that causes its length to fluctuate.
source: Thus, slow cycles of attachment and detachment lead to slowly varying force on the spindle that causes its length to fluctuate.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Short-lived kinetochore-MT attachment causes relatively quick turnover, limiting interkinetochore stretch, inward force, and variation in inward force.
source: In the opposite limit, short-lived kinetochore-MT attachment causes relatively quick turnover, limiting interkinetochore stretch, inward force, and variation in inward force.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Altered kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime could be a downstream effect that may result from the diverse mutations observed to cause spindle length fluctuations in S. pombe.
source: This analysis suggests that altered kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime could be a downstream effect that may result from the diverse mutations observed to cause spindle length fluctuations in S. pombe.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The effect of lifetime may not be the only source of spindle length fluctuations: other mutations that lead to slow changes in force exerted on the spindle could have similar effects.
source: We note that the effect of lifetime may not be the only source of spindle length fluctuations: other mutations that lead to slow changes in force exerted on the spindle could have similar effects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins.
source: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Hepperla et al., 2014), and chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness (Chacón et al., 2014; Nannas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length perturbations.

claim: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness.
source: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Hepperla et al., 2014), and chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness (Chacón et al., 2014; Nannas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length perturbations.

claim: It can be challenging to distinguish direct from indirect effects of altering force balance.
source: However, it can be challenging to distinguish direct from indirect effects of altering force balance.
evidence: This is a general statement about the difficulty of interpreting experimental results.

claim: In budding yeast, kinesin-14 deletion leads to shorter spindles, because kinesin-14 helps bundle spindle MTs, allowing kinesin-5 motors to generate greater outward force when kinesin-14 is present.
source: However, in budding yeast, kinesin-14 deletion instead leads to shorter spindles, because kinesin-14 helps bundle spindle MTs, allowing kinesin-5 motors to generate greater outward force when kinesin-14 is present (Hepperla et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinesin-14 function in budding yeast.

claim: Kinesin-8 deletion in fission yeast leads to longer spindles, but this is likely due to effects of this motor on MT dynamics rather than direct inward force generation by kinesin-8.
source: Similarly, kinesin-8 deletion in fission yeast leads to longer spindles, but this is likely due to effects of this motor on MT dynamics rather than direct inward force generation by kinesin-8 (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Gergely et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-8 function.

claim: For early time (up to 5 min) when spindles are short (up to 1 μm), motors and crosslinkers exert force that slowly increases in magnitude up to a few tens of pN, but chromosomes exert almost no force.
source: For early time (up to 5 min) when spindles are short (up to 1 μm), motors and crosslinkers exert force that slowly increases in magnitude up to a few tens of pN, but chromosomes exert almost no force (Figure 5C,F,I, Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model shown in Figure 5C,F,I and Video 7.

claim: Chromosomes do not exert significant inward force during initial SPB separation because they are not bioriented on the spindle.
source: Because chromosomes are not bioriented on the spindle during initial SPB separation, they do not exert significant inward force.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Initial bipolar spindle assembly can occur in a model lacking chromosomes.
source: This result is consistent with our previous work, which demonstrated that initial bipolar spindle assembly can occur in a model lacking chromosomes (Blackwell et al., 2017a; Rincon et al., 2017; Lamson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle assembly without chromosomes.

claim: The outward sliding force produced by kinesin-5 motors increases approximately linearly with spindle length, as the length of antiparallel MT overlaps increases during spindle assembly.
source: The outward sliding force produced by kinesin-5 motors increases approximately linearly with spindle length, as the length of antiparallel MT overlaps increases during spindle assembly (Figure 5D,G,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model shown in Figure 5D,G,J.

claim: The sliding force generated by kinesin-5 motors is proportional to overlap length.
source: This agrees with the experimental result that the sliding force generated by kinesin-5 motors is proportional to overlap length (Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinesin-5 force generation.

claim: The inward force generated by kinesin-14 motors is small.
source: The inward force generated by kinesin-14 motors is small, as in previous work that has shown that kinesin-14 is less effective at force generation that kinesin-5 (Hentrich and Surrey, 2010) and that in the spindle kinesin-14 may be more important to align spindle MTs than to generate force directly (Hepperla et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-14 force generation.

claim: Kinesin-14 is less effective at force generation than kinesin-5.
source: The inward force generated by kinesin-14 motors is small, as in previous work that has shown that kinesin-14 is less effective at force generation that kinesin-5 (Hentrich and Surrey, 2010) and that in the spindle kinesin-14 may be more important to align spindle MTs than to generate force directly (Hepperla et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinesin-14 force generation.

claim: In the spindle kinesin-14 may be more important to align spindle MTs than to generate force directly.
source: The inward force generated by kinesin-14 motors is small, as in previous work that has shown that kinesin-14 is less effective at force generation that kinesin-5 (Hentrich and Surrey, 2010) and that in the spindle kinesin-14 may be more important to align spindle MTs than to generate force directly (Hepperla et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinesin-14 function.

claim: During initial spindle assembly, crosslinkers play the primary role of maintaining antiparallel MT overlaps in opposition to the sliding activity of kinesin-5.
source: During initial spindle assembly, crosslinkers play the primary role of maintaining antiparallel MT overlaps in opposition to the sliding activity of kinesin-5.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The inward force generated by passive crosslinkers initially increases with spindle length to approximately 25 pN when the spindle is 0.75 μm long.
source: Remarkably, we find that the inward force generated by passive crosslinkers initially increases with spindle length to approximately 25 pN when the spindle is 0.75 μm long.
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model.

claim: Beyond 0.75 μm spindle length, the crosslinker force steadily decreases, dropping to near zero within a few minutes.
source: Beyond this point, the crosslinker force steadily decreases, dropping to near zero within a few minutes (Figure 5C,F,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model shown in Figure 5C,F,I.

claim: The crosslinker Ase1 generates large force for small overlaps that drops significantly as overlaps become larger.
source: This is consistent with previous results on force generation by the crosslinker Ase1, which found large force for small overlaps that drops significantly as overlaps become larger (Lansky et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Ase1 force generation.

claim: Early spindle assembly is characterized by high braking force by crosslinkers on short antiparallel MT overlaps opposing the outward force generated by kinesin-5.
source: Therefore, our results support a picture of early spindle assembly in which high braking force by crosslinkers on short antiparallel MT overlaps oppose the outward force generated by kinesin-5.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Crosslinkers play a key role in early spindle assembly.
source: This highlights the key role of crosslinkers in early spindle assembly suggested previously (Blackwell et al., 2017a; Rincon et al., 2017; Lamson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Once the spindle elongates sufficiently to separate SPBs by 1 μm, there is a transition in the primary contributer to spindle force.
source: Once the spindle elongates sufficiently to separate SPBs by 1 μm, there is a transition in the primary contributer to spindle force.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Chromosomes biorient and the inward force from interkinetochore stretch becomes significant, balancing outward force from kinesin-5 motors.
source: In this regime, chromosomes biorient and the inward force from interkinetochore stretch becomes significant, balancing outward force from kinesin-5 motors (Figure 5C,F,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model shown in Figure 5C,F,I.

claim: The balance between inward force from interkinetochore stretch and outward force from kinesin-5 motors is crucial to setting metaphase spindle length.
source: This balance is crucial to setting metaphase spindle length.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: When attachment is restricted, chromosomes rarely biorient and the inward force from chromosomes is small for spindles of all length.
source: When attachment is restricted, chromosomes rarely biorient and the inward force from chromosomes is small for spindles of all length.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Restricted attachment leads to unbalanced force from kinesin-5 motors and long spindles.
source: This leads to unbalanced force from kinesin-5 motors and long spindles (Figure 5E–G, Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5E–G and Video 7.

claim: When MT rescue is reduced, interkinetochore stretch is larger and the inward force from stretched sister kinetochores increases.
source: When MT rescue is reduced, interkinetochore stretch is larger and the inward force from stretched sister kinetochores increases (Figure 5H–J, Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5H–J and Video 7.

claim: Reduced MT rescue leads to shorter metaphase spindle length and a corresponding increase in force from stretched kinetochores.
source: This leads to shorter metaphase spindle length and a corresponding increase in force from stretched kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Relatively few changes are required for robust chromosome segregation in the model, suggesting that significant new mechanisms are not required in anaphase for chromosome segregation.
source: Relatively few changes are required for robust chromosome segregation, suggesting that significant new mechanisms are not required in anaphase for chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The rules added to the model for anaphase A include severing the chromatin spring between kinetochores (based on cumulative time the chromosomes are bioriented), stabilization of kinetochore-MT attachment, and depolymerization of MTs.
source: The rules added to the model for anaphase A include severing the chromatin spring between kinetochores (based on cumulative time the chromosomes are bioriented), stabilization of kinetochore-MT attachment, and depolymerization of MTs (Table 7).
evidence: This is a description of the model construction for anaphase.

claim: With the additions to the model for anaphase, simulations consistently segregate chromosomes to the poles.
source: With these additions to the model, simulations consistently segregate chromosomes to the poles (Figure 6A–D, Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A–D and Video 8.

claim: Simulations show similar speed of chromosome movement to the poles and separation of sisters as experimental measurements.
source: We compared our simulations to experimental measurements of chromosome segregation, and found similar speed of chromosome movement to the poles and separation of sisters (Figure 6E–G), as expected from the choice of MT depolymerization speed in the anaphase model.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: The computational model of mitosis can biorient chromosomes as the spindle assembles.
source: The computational model of mitosis presented here can biorient chromosomes as the spindle assembles.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The model was refined with experimental data on spindle structure, spindle elongation, and chromosome movements in fission yeast, leading to quantitative agreement with the data.
source: Our model was refined with experimental data on spindle structure, spindle elongation, and chromosome movements in fission yeast, leading to quantitative agreement with the data (Figure 2; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: The reference model results match previous genetics that found that kinesin-5 motors and CLASP are essential for bipolar spindle assembly.
source: The reference model results match previous genetics that found that kinesin-5 motors and CLASP are essential for bipolar spindle assembly (Hagan and Yanagida, 1990; Hagan and Yanagida, 1992; Bratman and Chang, 2007; Blackwell et al., 2017a), which suggests that the model captures key features needed to provide insight into mitotic mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to previous genetic studies.

claim: Inclusion of progressive restriction in the model was motivated by recent work on the monopolin complex in fission yeast and attachment-driven compaction of mammalian kinetochores.
source: Inclusion of this effect in the model was motivated by recent work on the monopolin complex in fission yeast (Gregan et al., 2007) and attachment-driven compaction of mammalian kinetochores (Magidson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore geometry.

claim: Progressive restriction promotes proper attachment by favoring binding of microtubules from the same pole that is already attached to the kinetochore.
source: Progressive restriction has two key effects: it promotes proper attachment by favoring binding of microtubules from the same pole that is already attached to the kinetochore, and simultaneously creates a torque that helps to reorient the kinetochore on the spindle.
evidence: This is an inference from the model construction and simulation results.

claim: Progressive restriction creates a torque that helps to reorient the kinetochore on the spindle.
source: Progressive restriction has two key effects: it promotes proper attachment by favoring binding of microtubules from the same pole that is already attached to the kinetochore, and simultaneously creates a torque that helps to reorient the kinetochore on the spindle.
evidence: This is an inference from the model construction and simulation results.

claim: The monopolin complex components Pcs1/Mde4 were found not to be essential in fission yeast.
source: In previous work, the monopolin complex components Pcs1/Mde4 were found not to be essential in fission yeast (Gregan et al., 2007), but in our model completely removing progressive restriction abolishes biorientation (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on monopolin.

claim: In fission yeast, other molecules may contribute to progressive restriction in addition to monopolin.
source: This suggests the possibility that in fission yeast, other molecules may contribute to progressive restriction in addition to monopolin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results and previous literature.

claim: Destabilization by approximately a factor of 70 gives the highest degree of biorientation in the model.
source: Destabilization by approximately a factor of 70 gives the highest degree of biorientation the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The degree of destabilization that gives the highest biorientation in the model is similar to the degree of destabilization previously estimated to occur due to Aurora B.
source: This is similar to the degree of destabilization previously estimated to occur due to Aurora B (Cimini et al., 2006), further suggesting that the model produces biologically relevant results.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to previous literature.

claim: Without force dependence of attachment, kinetochores frequently detach from depolymerizing MTs and lose biorientation.
source: Without this force dependence, kinetochores frequently detach from depolymerizing MTs and lose biorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The model achieves biorientation for the longest time with an increased force-sensitivity of attachment compared to experimental measurements.
source: Our model achieves biorientation for the longest time with an increased force-sensitivity of attachment compared to experimental measurements, a difference that would be of interest to explore in future work.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental measurements.

claim: The timing of spindle assembly and biorientation in the model were consistent with those quantified experimentally.
source: The timing of spindle assembly and biorientation in the model were consistent with those quantified experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data.

claim: A current difference between the model and experiment is that the model finds ongoing turnover of kinetochore-MT attachments, so that biorientation can be lost once established.
source: A current difference between the model and experiment is that we find ongoing turnover of kinetochore-MT attachments, so that biorientation can be lost once established.
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results to experimental observations.

claim: Previous experimental work suggests that for metaphase spindles, once biorientation is established it is rarely lost.
source: This is in contrast to previous experimental work, which suggests that for metaphase spindles, once biorientation is established it is rarely lost (Waters et al., 1996; Nicklas, 1997; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on biorientation stability.

claim: In S. pombe, a relatively small number of kinetochores and MTs contribute to spindle length, and therefore the changing force on the three chromosomes can have a significant effect on the spindle.
source: Our results suggest why large spindle length fluctuations have not been seen in larger spindles in vertebrate cells: in S. pombe, a relatively small number of kinetochores and MTs contribute to spindle length, and therefore the changing force on the three chromosomes can have a significant effect on the spindle.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: In vertebrate spindles with tens of thousands of MTs, changes in force on a small number of kinetochores contribute only a small fractional change to overall force on the spindle, leading to smaller fluctuations.
source: In vertebrate spindles with tens of thousands of MTs, changes in force on a small number of kinetochores contribute only a small fractional change to overall force on the spindle, leading to smaller fluctuations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The early spindle has almost no force generation from interkinetochore stretch because chromosomes are rarely bioriented at this stage.
source: The early spindle has almost no force generation from interkinetochore stretch because chromosomes are rarely bioriented at this stage.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The early spindle is characterized by outward force from kinesin-5 motors that is resisted by crosslinkers.
source: Instead, the early spindle is characterized by outward force from kinesin-5 motors that is resisted by crosslinkers.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The force from crosslinkers is highest when MT antiparallel overlaps are short and drops as the spindle elongates.
source: Consistent with earlier work (Lansky et al., 2015), the force from crosslinkers is highest when MT antiparallel overlaps are short and drops as the spindle elongates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and simulation results.

claim: Once the bipolar spindle is formed and chromosomes are bioriented, attached chromosomes provide significant inward force that opposes the outward force of kinesin-5 motors.
source: Once the bipolar spindle is formed and chromosomes are bioriented, attached chromosomes provide significant inward force that opposes the outward force of kinesin-5 motors.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The many mutations that alter spindle length in fission yeast might act indirectly by altering kinesin-5 force generation or interkinetochore stretch.
source: These results suggest that the many mutations that alter spindle length in fission yeast (Syrovatkina et al., 2013) might act indirectly by altering kinesin-5 force generation or interkinetochore stretch.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The model is able to transition to anaphase A and robustly segregate chromosomes to the poles with a small number of additional rules.
source: Remarkably, the model is able to transition to anaphase A and robustly segregate chromosomes to the poles with a small number of additional rules (Figure 6; Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6 and Video 8.

claim: The work provides a powerful framework for testing spindle assembly mechanisms that can inform future experimental studies.
source: Overall, our work provides a powerful framework for testing spindle assembly mechanisms that can inform future experimental studies.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the value of the work.
